6735.etyen:
Compound of b (“B-flat”) + moll (“minor key”), literally “B-flat minor”.
The first element b (“B-flat”) is the musical note a semitone below h (“B natural”). Its use in this sense reflects the medieval distinction between b molle (“soft B”) and b durum (“hard B”). The second element moll (“minor key”) is through German Moll (“minor key”), from Medieval Latin molle (“soft”), the neuter of Latin mollis (“soft, mild”). The deeper Indo-European ancestry of the Latin word is disputed.
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk b-moll, Danish b-mol, Swedish b-moll, German b-Moll, Finnish b-mo

Hvis det kommer en ♭ på en tone, får den endelsen -ess, når man utaler den.
If a ♭ is added to a note, it receives the ending -ess when pronounced.

1000271.etyen:
Borrowed from German -es (“semitone-lowering suffix; flat”). The German musical suffix belongs to a note-naming convention that developed from German organ tablature. An e-shaped sign appended to note letters was derived from Tironian shorthand, in which such signs represented word-final -is or -es. The convention became lexicalized in German note names, producing forms such as Cis and Fis for raised notes and Des and Ges for lowered notes. Norwegian adapted the lowering suffix as -ess.
The corresponding raising suffix is -iss, likewise based on German -is. Compare also the shortened lowering

a male given name from Old Norse Eiríkr, equivalent to English Eric

1001295.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Eiríkr (“male given name”), from Proto-Norse *Aina-rīkijaʀ (“sole ruler”) or *Aiwa-rīkijaʀ (“everlasting ruler”). In the first and usual Norwegian interpretation, the first element is from *ainaz (“one, alone, unique”); an alternative connects it with *aiwaz (“age, eternity”). The second element is from *rīkijaz (“kingly, powerful, rich; ruler”). The spelling preserves the diphthong of Old Norse Eiríkr, unlike the monophthongized form Erik.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Eirik, Icelandic Eiríkur, Faroese Eirikur, Danish Erik, Swedish Erik, English Eric and German Erich.

uf da! Hug han ikke fingren af!
Oh dear! Do not chop his finger off!

1002063.etyen:
From uff (“interjection expressing alarm, discomfort, regret, etc.”) + da (“unstressed affective particle”).
The first element is onomatopoeic or sound-symbolic; compare huff (“interjection expressing discomfort, dismay, exasperation, etc.”), likewise a sound word with substantially overlapping uses. In this unstressed affective use after interjections and strong expressions, da continues Old Norse þó (“nevertheless, still”), rather than the temporal adverb þá (“then, at that time”).

en.g: good day, hello; a greeting equivalent to god dag (“good day”)
x: Goddagen, sier morfar. – God dag, sier jeg

1005135.etyen:
Compound of god (“good”) + dag (“day”) with the definite singular ending -en (“the”) on the second element, literally “the good day”.
God (“good”) is from Old Norse góðr (“good”), from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz (“good”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to join, unite, suit”). Dag (“day”) is from Old Norse dagr (“day”), from Proto-Germanic *dagaz (“day”). Its further origin is uncertain.
